name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
role: Indian nationalist leader, journalist and teacher (1856–1920)
summary: Tilak led the radical 'Extremist' wing of the Indian National Congress, demanding swaraj through boycott, Swadeshi and national education, and later self-government within the British Empire through the Home Rule League. He mixed religious and cultural revival (the Shivaji and Ganapati festivals) with mass politics, backed decentralised village self-government and the right to bear arms, and held conservative views on marriage law.

notes: Themes searched: colonial rule and self-government, Swadeshi and boycott, tariffs and industry, education and language, religion and caste, Hindu-Muslim relations and electorates, violence and legal agitation, arms and the war, decentralisation, courts, marriage and women. Sources were the 1922 collection of his speeches and articles, the 1908 trial report, and Oak's 2022 Leiden thesis, which quotes his Marathi writings. His Marathi Kesari articles in full, the Gita Rahasya text and Congress reports were not searched. Economy, ecology, technology, most liberty and world statements found no stated position. His views on violence and legal methods shifted between his radical years (1890s-1908) and after his 1914 release; both are recorded as mixed.
